content: Arthritis, derived from the Greek words arthromeaning joint and -itis meaning inflammation, refers to painful damage to the joints. It can manifest as part of a systemic disorder or involve a single joint. Common symptoms include joint pain (arthralgia), swelling, redness (erythema), warmth, and restricted movement. Arthritis can be classified based on the number of joints involved, the presence of inflammation, or the duration of symptoms. Osteoarthritis, also known as degenerative joint disease, is the most prevalent form of arthritis in the United States, affecting up to 10% of individuals over the age of 60. Inflammatory arthritis is frequently associated with systemic autoimmune disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). In these systemic conditions, the disease course is typically chronic, and multiple joints (polyarticular) are often affected. In contrast, infectious conditions like septic arthritis are acute in nature and usually involve a single joint (monoarticular). Crystal-induced arthropathies, such as gout, result from the deposition of uric acid crystals in the joint space, leading to inflammatory joint involvement. While the disease course and systemic manifestations are important for diagnosis, the gold standard for confirming arthritis involves joint aspiration, fluid analysis, and microscopic evaluation. Imaging studies can also be useful in certain cases to assess the chronicity of the disease and structural changes in the joint and surrounding tissues. Prompt treatment is essential, particularly for septic and inflammatory conditions, to prevent structural joint damage and deformities. Primary Forms of Arthritis: Osteoarthritis Rheumatoid arthritis Septic arthritis Gout and pseudogout Juvenile idiopathic arthritis Still's disease Ankylosing spondylitis Differential Diagnosis of Monoarthritis: To explore the differential diagnosis of monoarthritis with specific symptoms, such as joint swelling, fever, weight loss, claudication, morning stiffness, local erythema, or combinations of these, further detailed resources are available. Differential Diagnosis of Polyarthritis: Similarly, for polyarthritis, the differential diagnosis can be reviewed based on symptoms like joint swelling, fever, weight loss, claudication, morning stiffness, local erythema, or combinations of these.
